blockinfile automatically wraps its inserted content in # BEGIN ANSIBLE MANAGED BLOCK / # END ANSIBLE MANAGED BLOCK comment markers, specifically so re-running the task is idempotent — it can find and replace its own previous block instead of appending duplicates. The marker parameter lets you customize those comment characters for file types that don't use #.

🎯 RHCE-RELEVANT Always set state explicitly (present or absent) even when a module's documentation lists a default — module defaults have changed between versions before, and an explicit state makes the playbook's INTENT unambiguous to the next person (or future you) reading it.

A template is a source file that gets customized for each managed host at deploy time, using variables and facts — instead of a static file that's identical everywhere. Ansible uses the Jinja2 templating engine, the same one used for variable references inside playbooks themselves.
Output — renders a variable or expression's VALUE into the file
Logic — loops, conditionals; produces no visible output itself
A comment — stripped entirely from the rendered output, never shown to the end user
A template file needs no particular extension to work — .j2 is just a strong convention that makes template files instantly recognizable in a project.
# DO NOT MAKE LOCAL MODIFICATIONS TO THIS FILE AS THEY WILL BE LOST

💡 WHY THIS MATTERS This one template file can produce a DIFFERENT sshd_config for every managed host — different listen address per host automatically (from facts), different port/policy per host or group (from variables) — while staying a single, readable, version-controlled source file instead of dozens of near-identical hand-maintained configs.
Deploying a template with the template module

Like copy and file, the template module also accepts owner, group, mode, and SELinux context. It additionally supports validate, which runs an arbitrary command against the rendered file BEFORE it's put in place — e.g. validate: 'visudo -c -f %s' rejects a broken sudoers file instead of deploying it and breaking sudo.

A best practice: include a comment at the top of every template noting it's Ansible-managed, so nobody wastes time hand-editing a file that will just be overwritten on the next play run. The ansible_managed directive (set in ansible.cfg) provides ready-made text for exactly this:

🎯 RHCE-RELEVANT This is one of the most exam-relevant facts in the whole chapter: Jinja2 for-loops and if-conditionals work INSIDE TEMPLATE FILES, but NOT inside Ansible playbooks. Playbooks get their iteration and branching from the loop and when task keywords covered in Part 3 — a template's for/if are a completely separate mechanism that only exists inside .j2 files.

hostvars[host] (from Part 2's magic variables) is what makes this possible — each pass through the loop reaches into a DIFFERENT host's facts, letting one template describe every host in the inventory at once.

The line inside only appears in the rendered file at all if finished evaluates true — this is a genuinely different mechanism from a task's when, which decides whether the WHOLE TASK runs, not which lines of a file get written.

✗ COMMON MISTAKE Confusing a Jinja2 FILTER (| to_json, transforms a value) with a Jinja2 TEST (is failed, returns true/false, used in conditions). They use different syntax (pipe vs. is) and solve different problems — one reshapes data, the other asks a yes/no question about it.

Deploy a per-host-customized configuration via a Jinja2 template that loops over the inventory, and manage a supporting file with the Files modules.

Every host in your small inventory needs an /etc/hosts file listing every OTHER host by IP, hostname, and FQDN — generated automatically instead of hand-maintained. Separately, each host needs a marked banner block added to /etc/motd, and a stale legacy file removed.
An inventory of at least three hosts, all in the [all] group, reachable with facts gatherable
A pre-existing /etc/legacy-app.conf on each host that should no longer exist
1. Write templates/hosts.j2 using a Jinja2 for loop over groups['all'] to generate IP/FQDN/hostname lines for every host, prefixed with an ansible_managed comment
2. Deploy it to /etc/hosts with the template module
3. Use blockinfile to add a banner block to /etc/motd on every host
4. Use the file module to ensure /etc/legacy-app.conf does NOT exist, with state made explicit
5. Run the playbook twice and confirm the second run reports ok (not changed) for every task

Remember the exam-critical distinction from Section 4.3: the for loop belongs INSIDE the .j2 template file, not inside the playbook's tasks: list. The playbook task itself is just a normal template: call with no loop keyword needed.

Before checking the solution: did you accidentally try to put {% for %} inside the playbook YAML instead of the template file? That's the single most common mistake when first learning this chapter — the playbook stays simple; all the looping logic lives in the .j2 file.
- name: Fleet hosts file and housekeeping
This system is managed by Ansible.
hostvars[host] inside the for loop reaches into EACH host's own gathered facts in turn — this is what lets one template describe the whole fleet.
blockinfile's automatic BEGIN/END markers are what make the second run report ok instead of duplicating the banner text.
state: absent on the file task is explicit on purpose — matching Section 4.1's guidance to always state intent clearly rather than relying on a module default.

cat /etc/hosts on any host should list every OTHER host's real IP/FQDN/hostname, sourced from facts, not hardcoded. A second playbook run should show changed=0 across the board — proof the template, the blockinfile markers, and the file removal are all correctly idempotent.

Generating /etc/hosts (or similar fleet-wide reference files) from live inventory facts is a genuinely common real pattern — it means the file is always accurate the moment a host is added to or removed from the inventory, with zero manual synchronization required.
Q1. What's the key difference between lineinfile/blockinfile and templating an entire file?

Answer: lineinfile/blockinfile patch part of an existing file (fragile for complex changes); a template generates the WHOLE file fresh each run from variables/facts, which is more reliable and readable for anything beyond a small tweak.
Q2. Which module is the reverse of copy, pulling a file FROM a managed host back to the control node?
Q3. What does copy's default force: yes actually do?
Answer: Overwrites the remote file's content if it differs from the source file, every run — set force: no to only copy when the destination doesn't already exist.
Q4. How does blockinfile achieve idempotence across repeated runs?
Answer: It wraps its inserted content in automatic BEGIN/END comment markers, letting it find and replace its own previous block instead of appending duplicates.
Q5. What are the three Jinja2 delimiter types, and what does each do?
Answer: {{ }} outputs a value; {% %} contains logic (loops/conditionals); {# #} is a comment, stripped from output entirely.
Q6. Can Jinja2 {% for %} loops be used directly inside an Ansible playbook's tasks list?
Answer: No — Jinja2 for-loops and if-conditionals work only INSIDE template files; playbooks use the loop and when task keywords instead.
Q7. What does the ansible_managed directive provide, and where is it configured?
Answer: Standard text (set in ansible.cfg) meant to be placed in a template's header comment, warning that the file is managed by Ansible and shouldn't be hand-edited.
Q8. What does the validate option on the template module do?
Answer: Runs an arbitrary command against the RENDERED file before it's put in place, letting you reject a broken config (e.g. visudo -c) instead of deploying it.
Q9. What's the difference between a Jinja2 filter and a Jinja2 test?
Answer: A filter (| to_json) transforms/reshapes a value's output format; a test (is failed) asks a true/false question about a value, typically inside a when condition.
Q10. In a template that loops with hostvars[host][...], what does hostvars make possible that plain ansible_facts alone couldn't?

Answer: Reaching into ANOTHER host's facts from within a single template render — letting one file (like a generated /etc/hosts) describe every host in the inventory, not just the one it's being deployed to.
RH294 — RED HAT SYSTEM ADMINISTRATION III: LINUX AUTOMATION

This Part covers RH294 Chapter 7 in full: precisely targeting hosts with pattern syntax, dynamic inventories for environments that change too fast for a static file, tuning how many hosts Ansible touches at once, and splitting large playbooks into manageable, reusable pieces.

💡 WHY THIS MATTERS Everything so far has run against a handful of lab hosts. This Part is about what changes once you're managing dozens or hundreds of real servers — targeting exactly the right subset, not hammering them all at once, and not maintaining one unmanageable 2,000-line playbook file.
